posts.author: ron olson
posts.content_md:
Thank you for changing the tone of this forum section away from "Dumpster Diving for Pulsed Lasers". If you have some extra time and a little money - have you given thought to augmenting your laser (actually replacing the final amplifier ) with Nd:Silicate Glass? The problem with using a small diameter (6mm) Nd:YAG rod for the power amplifier is that it becomes an unwanted aperture in the beam. As a rough approximation: 5-10% of the energy reaching the rod edge will result in ~ 30-40% spatial modulation. Getting rid of these rings will require spatial filtering or (easier) using the beam in the true far-field : allowing several meters for the beam to propogate back to Gaussian. This is costly with respect to energy. I see 1/2" diameter and 5/8" diameter (typically x 8" long) amplifier glass and ruby heads/power supplies from time to time on Laserresale.com and with your experience, integration shouldn't be a problem. You may have to keep the gain down to avoid free-running (lasing outside the Q-switched window) but with ~200mJ input (from your first Nd:YAG amp stage) you should be able to get at least 1J output without stressing the system and this should translate to a nice 300-400mJ single shot green output capable of exposing 24" x 20" plates. 

As an aside for holographers using Q-switched Nd:YAG or Nd:YLF- I recently tested both the new Fuji film (FH L) and the new HF 55 film from Filmotec. Both produced good initial test results in reflection using ~500mJ in15ns @532nm with SM-6 developer and PBU Amidol bleach.

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
Hi Ron,

I agree with you the final stage has the limiting aperture of the 1/4 rod and was a known issue before design. But was a demonstration of some available parts. The parameters around this laser was to work within an integrated head/power supply unit which Nd:yag afforded some efficiencies regarding size but lower energy storage than the silicate. Nd:yag oscillators also was known to have it's own issues related to depolarizaton so this was an attempt to quantify a moderate output system using such rods. The system is still undergoing revisions to achieve it's goals. But as such, it's design criteria still is a small chassis system. If other design factors like limited life electrolytics are totally incorporated it may still be possible to use a glass amplifier in this system. No calculations yet have been made regarding that although some consideration already had been given to larger aperture Nd:yag rod 2nd stage if the part become available at a reasonable price. Thank you for your comments and you offered a very good suggestion. 

Dear Han, 

Many researchers's technical papers have referred to their use of "Solid State Laser Engineering" by Walter Koechner. This is a good technical reference book with distillation of many technical references.

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
Dear Hans,

A reasonable budget for a frugal shopper and experienced builder. Many sources exist for finding quality parts at a low price. If you are doing this to learn about lasers, the years of effort and study may be worth it. But these systems are dangerous and power supplies are lethal. I'll refer to my earlier ranting: [http://www.holographyforum.org/phpBB2/v ... php?t=4514](http://www.holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=4514) If I felt I didn't have the proper experience, I would undertake a dpss project instead since there is plenty of technical challenge there to obtain a single mode laser and at a much safer voltage. Pulse systems can be built from low voltage diodes, but the cost would beyond most people's means. Okay not sure that at all helps, but I'm compelled to tell you.
